entries.note: Itself slang and of uncertain origin; theories include French [[from?:langue]], Scots slang 'to linger', a back-formation from [[from?:slanger]], a past participle of [[from?:sling]], or slangs, fetters.
A Nordic phrase implying verbal abuse, probably not the source of [[see:slang]] though perhaps related to slinging words around.
Nineteenth-century American English for someone who uses abusive [[see:slang]], or a ranting partisan.
Criminal slang deliberately designed to be obscure to outsiders, from the Latin for sing, like chanting.
Another term for criminal slang, a French word of unknown origin, sometimes pronounced 'argo'.
One of the more linguistic terms for [[see:cant]] and slang, implying a language used within a particular circle.
A linguistic term for slang or [[see:cant]], implying a language used within a particular circle or for a particular purpose.
A linguistic term for slang or [[see:cant]], implying a language used within a particular circle or for a particular purpose.
A linguistic term for slang or [[see:cant]], implying a language used within a particular circle or for a particular purpose.
A linguistic term for slang or [[see:cant]], implying a language used within a particular circle or for a particular purpose.
Underground gay London slang of the 20th century, developed from criminal and entertainers' slang, with strong Italian influence; covered in an earlier episode.
Slang uses date to the 1700s; the stylish, approving sense came from 1920s black American music culture, recorded in [[see:Zora Neale Hurston]] in 1933.
Recorded from 1721; probably a large sum fully counted, so no longer active or hot.
Calm under pressure, an early use of [[see:cool]] that mirrors [[see:hotheaded]].
Also dates back relatively far, explaining the sense of [[see:coolheaded]].
Shows up around 1918, part of the 20th-century stylish sense of [[see:cool]].
1940s US jazz slang for a stiff, old-fashioned person, the antithesis of [[see:cool]], building on [[from:square toes]] and [[see:square meal]].
From the 1800s, a full substantial meal; in the US 'a square' alone could also mean one.
From 1752, a precise or old-fashioned person, after an early 18th-century men's shoe style; earlier cousin of [[gave:square]].
Quite literal: from the grooves in a record, as in being [[see:in the groove]].
Being with the music, like a stylus in the groove, explaining [[see:groovy]].
From 1828, meaning excellent, from [[from:supernaculum]], wine good enough to drink to the last drop.
Sham Latin from a drinking game where drops spilling from the thumbnail meant refilling; an excellent wine, source of [[gave:supernacular]].

entries.term: all wool and a yard wide
entries.note: 1800s idiom for genuine or trustworthy, since cheap cloth of scrap fibres like [[see:shoddy]] was narrower than the standard yard.
Scrap fibres used in cheap fabric, mentioned in explaining [[see:all wool and a yard wide]]; discussed in an earlier episode.
Something excellent; originally American but sounds British, popularised in England by [[see:David Dickinson]] on Bargain Hunt.
Presenter of the antiques show Bargain Hunt who would call finds 'a real [[see:bobby-dazzler]]'.
Turn-of-the-century abbreviation for 'very highly commended', like something on a school report.
Southernism for a boisterous good time, probably a twist on [[from?:rip-roaring]] adding a horse or cow's snort.
Slightly older term for something boisterous and violent, likely the model for [[gave?:rip-snorting]].
Credit, respect or approval, short for [[from:propers]].
Used by [[see:Aretha Franklin]] in [[see:Respect]], the clearest bridge to [[gave:props]], per Ben Zimmer, after which the OED updated its entry.
Sang 'give me my [[see:propers]]', and varied songs each time, making lip-syncing hard in [[see:The Blues Brothers]].
The [[see:Aretha Franklin]] song containing the line 'give me my [[see:propers]]'.
Film in which [[see:Aretha Franklin]] was hard to shoot because she sang slightly differently every time.
Rob tests Jess with examples from a Victorian glossary, often based on famous people, foods and London places, sometimes layering slang on slang.
Carried to Australia by transported criminals, sharing some [[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] but developing its own terms in New South Wales and beyond.
Victorian [[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for yes.
Victorian [[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for no.
A mint sweet from Everton in Liverpool, used as rhyming slang for coffee.
London place name used as rhyming slang for arm, so your arms are your 'chalks'.
Rhyming slang for horse, since it was pronounced 'Chering Cross' back then; Jess guessed it via [[see:hoss]].
American slang short for horse, which led Jess to guess [[see:Charing Cross]].
Rhyming slang for a shilling, from Britain's old non-decimal money.
Rhyming slang for a shilling, a lazier-sounding alternative to [[see:Abraham's willing]].
Rhyming slang for a [[see:deuce]], itself slang for twopence.
Slang for a twopenny piece, rhymed by [[see:bottle of spruce]].
Rhyming slang for [[see:thrums]], a threepenny piece.
Slang for a threepenny piece, rhymed by [[see:currants and plums]].
Rhyming slang for a [[see:brown]], a penny.
Nickname for a penny, rhymed by [[see:Camden Town]].
Rhyming slang for a [[see:farden]], a farthing.
Dialect way of saying farthing, rhymed by [[see:Covent Garden]].
Rhyming slang for a [[see:tanner]], a sixpence.
Slang for a sixpence, rhymed by [[see:goddess Diana]].
Rhyming slang for a hat, via [[see:tile]], Cockney for hat: slang on slang.
Cockney for a hat, as in the song [[see:Any Old Iron]], rhymed by [[see:battle of the Nile]].
Song Rob sings to illustrate [[see:tile]] meaning a hat.
Australian rhyming slang for a pub.
Australian rhyming slang for an immigrant, shortened to Jimmy; it rhymes all the way through, a [[see:rime riche]].
French name for an extra-strong rhyme like [[see:Jimmy Grant]], rhyming more than once.
Australian rhyming slang for a look, only coinable in the Antipodes.
Australian rhyming slang originally for a nark that came to mean a shark.
Australian rhyming slang for nice, so someone could be described as 'apples'.
To vomit, now in British English; thought to come from [[from?:Chunder Loo of Akim Foo]], rhyming slang for spew.
Cartoon character from an advert, thought to be rhyming slang for spew and the source of [[gave?:chunder]].
Australian rhyming slang meaning to bolt or disappear, also 'doing a Harry', after Prime Minister [[from:Harold Holt]].
Australian prime minister who vanished, presumed drowned, while swimming off Victoria in 1967, inspiring [[gave:do a Harold Holt]].
American slang first found in pre-Civil War Midwestern dialect, possibly from northern English [[from?:scaddle]], to scare; spread via 1860s reports of fleeing Confederates.
Older American frontier term from the 1830s, from Spanish [[from:vamos]], let's go; less about running away than [[see:skedaddle]].
Left [[see:Polari]] for broader English as slang for a toilet, from Italian [[from:casa]], house, via criminal slang.
[[see:Polari]] for a gay man, from [[from:omi]] and palone.
[[see:Polari]] for man, from the Italian for man; found in [[gave:omi-palone]] and [[gave:naff omi]].
Dreary; the 'not available for effing' acronym is a rationalisation; likely from Italian [[from?:nafa]]; early use by [[see:Kenneth Williams]] about naff garden gnomes.
[[see:Polari]] for a dreary man, combining [[from:naff]] and [[from:omi]].
Gay comedian whose Polari-speaking character on [[see:Round the Horne]] gives an early record of [[see:naff]].
Comedy show where [[see:Kenneth Williams]] used much Polari, often unnoticed by audiences who enjoyed the flowery words.
As in 'ate that up' or 'ate and left no crumbs', praise for an exceptional performance, from black and Latino gay slang in New York City.
Popularised by New York black and Latino gay slang, though it has been all over the place, making its spread hard to track.
Another term popularised by New York black and Latino gay slang, alongside [[see:slay]] and [[see:reading]].
Sharply, wittily pointing out someone's flaws, a form of [[see:roasting]], seen in reading challenges on [[see:RuPaul's Drag Race]]; extended in [[see:the library is open]].
Discussed in an earlier episode; the tea is the truth, also obliquely referencing trans identity, partly popularised by [[see:Lady Chablis]].
Mentioned in a previous episode as helping popularise [[see:spill the tea]].
Reality show featuring challenges built around [[see:reading]].
Extension of [[see:reading]] meaning you're ready to read people, tearing them apart wittily.
Compared with [[see:reading]], which is a different kind of roasting.
A way of speaking that inserts 'iz' and 'izzle' into words, like [[see:pig Latin]], showcased in [[see:Double Dutch Bus]]; source of [[gave:shizzle my nizzle]].
The -izzle usage associated with [[see:Snoop Dogg]], a spin-off of [[from:double Dutch]].
Rapper associated with the -izzle usage of [[see:shizzle my nizzle]].
Word-rearranging play language compared with [[see:double Dutch]].
1981 song by Frankie Smith with a middle section entirely in [[see:double Dutch]], which Rob recites and translates.
French slang swapping syllables, as in [[see:Stromae]]; similar to [[see:back slang]].
Belgian music artist whose name swaps the two syllables of maestro, an example of [[see:verlan]].
Slang made by reversing words, often twisted rather than straight reversals; source of everyday words like [[see:yob]].
British word for a hoodlum, [[see:back slang]] for boy.
Used among London Jews for a gentile, [[from:goy]] reversed.
A name, of otherwise unknown origin; one theory, noted by the OED, is [[see:back slang]] for 'name', the source of [[same-root?:nickname]].
From rebracketing 'an ekename' as 'a nickname', from the same 'name' theorised to give [[same-root?:moniker]].
[[see:back slang]] for seven.
[[see:back slang]] for four, usually a four-year prison sentence.
A fiver, five pounds or dollars, [[see:back slang]] of [[from:finif]], from the Yiddish for five, related to German fünf.
Wrestling's fake portrayal of real competition and beef, possibly [[see:back slang]] for 'be fake'.
[[see:back slang]] for woman, further twisted into longer plural forms.
[[see:back slang]] for look.
[[see:back slang]] for knife, a straight reversal.
[[see:back slang]] for girl.
[[see:back slang]] for police, partly switched around; gave [[gave:slop]].
Disparaging slang for police, from [[from:esclop]], because people disliked the police.
A mindset centred on the grind, seen on LinkedIn and loathed by Jess.
Millennial slang, though 'that's such a vibe' feels more Gen Z; now used differently grammatically.
Older slang for the aura around a person, now used differently; accumulated through [[see:aura farming]].
Internet slang for deliberately accumulating or displaying [[see:aura]], from video-game farming of points, here social prestige.
Compared with [[see:aura]]; Jess thinks it's already passé.
No longer fun for kids once adults and media picked it up; now mostly older generations joke about it.
Brainrot meme slang defined as doing something smart but risky, though not used that way; linked to the meme character [[see:Gurt]].
TikTok segment sharing brainrot memes packed with inside jokes, where [[see:gurting]] arose.
Older meme slang, imitative of something being thrown through the air.
Meme acronym for 'I'm a keep it a Gurt', from the same memes as [[see:gurting]].
Meme character who answers the word yogurt with 'yo', making [[see:gurting]] clearer.
Being bold or ready to go big, from action sports forums alongside [[see:send it]], before TikTok.
Action-sports slang for committing enthusiastically, related to [[see:getting sendy]].
Outclassing someone so they look inferior, from [[from:AMOG]]; spread beyond the manosphere via [[see:Clavicular]]; also hair- or jaw-mogged.
Manosphere acronym for 'alpha male of the group', a dominant attractive man, source of [[gave:mogging]].
Streamer famed for his jawline who was said to be [[see:frame-mogged]] by a judge in an alligator-shooting case.
Said of [[see:Clavicular]] when outclassed by a judge's physique, a variant of [[see:mogging]].
